scenes.title: Split around one value
scenes.narration: Quicksort is a divide and conquer sort. Here is a list of eight numbers.

steps.say: It picks one value, the pivot. In this version, the pivot is always the last item. Here that is five.
One split moves the smaller numbers to its left, and the bigger ones to its right.
The pivot is now exactly where it belongs in the sorted list. It never moves again.
The two sides are still jumbled, so quicksort splits each of them the same way.

scenes.title: Partition around the pivot 5
scenes.narration: Here is how one split works.

steps.say: The pointer j walks from left to right, comparing each number with the pivot.
The pointer i marks the end of the small pile. It starts just before the list.
j looks at seven. Seven is not smaller than five, so it stays put.
j moves on to two. Two is smaller than the pivot, so it belongs in the small pile.
So i steps forward, and the two swaps into the small pile.
Nine is bigger, so j just moves past it.
Four is smaller. The next spot in the small pile holds seven.
i steps forward, and four swaps places with the seven.
One is smaller too, and the next spot holds nine.
So one swaps with the nine.
Eight is bigger. Skip it.
Three is smaller, and the next spot holds seven.
Three swaps with the seven.
Every number before the pivot has been checked. The spot right after the small pile holds nine.
So the pivot and the nine swap.
Five lands at index four. Smaller on its left, bigger on its right.

scenes.narration: Now quicksort calls itself on the left side, then on the right. Each call gets a smaller piece.

steps.say: The left side runs from index zero to three. Its pivot is three.
After the split, three lands at index two.
Next, the piece from zero to one. Its pivot is one.
One is smaller than two, so it lands at index zero.
What is left are single items: the two, and the four. One item is already sorted, so the calls stop.
Now the three cells on the right. Their pivot is nine.
Eight and seven are both smaller, so nine stays at the end.
Then the pair left of it, with pivot seven.
Seven swaps in front of eight, and eight is left on its own.
Every pivot landed in its place. The whole list is sorted.

scenes.narration: Here is the same thing in Java: two short methods.

steps.label: stop when low < high is false
steps.say: quickSort first checks the base case. If low is not below high, the piece has one item or none.

steps.label: split, get the pivot spot
steps.say: Otherwise it splits the piece and gets back where the pivot landed.

steps.label: sort each side
steps.say: Then it sorts the part left of the pivot, and the part right of it.

steps.label: pivot is the last item
steps.say: partition takes the last item as the pivot, and starts i just before low.

steps.label: grow the small pile
steps.say: j walks from low up to the pivot. Each time it finds a smaller number, i steps forward and the two swap.

steps.label: put the pivot in place
steps.say: Last, the pivot swaps in right after the small pile, and partition returns that spot.

steps.say: So the speed depends on how many rounds there are.
When the pivot lands near the middle, each round halves the pieces.
Eight items take three rounds, which is log two of eight.
Each round costs n, so that gives n log n, both on average and at best.
But give it a list that is already sorted.
The last item is always the biggest, so each split peels off just one item.
That makes about n rounds, and the time grows with n squared. This is the worst case.
Quicksort sorted our list in place, with no second list.
Best and average are both n log n.
The worst case is n squared, when every pivot is the biggest or smallest item.
The only extra memory is the stack of calls waiting to finish.
